17662: Intensive properties (temperature, density, melting point, colour) do not depend on the amount of matter; extensive properties (mass, volume) do. Elements contain one kind of atom; compounds contain elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio (e.g. dry ice = CO₂); mixtures have variable composition (alloys such as brass, bronze, solder, mild steel).
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.2.4 Properties of Matter · p.14-15
17663: Solids have fixed shape and volume; liquids have fixed volume but take the shape of the container; gases fill the container. Liquids and gases can flow, so both are called fluids. Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.2.2 States of Matter · p.7-9
17664: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with other elements: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), solder (Sn + Pb), mild steel (Fe + C), stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni).
17665: Sedimentation: coarse particles settle under gravity. Decantation: pouring off the clear liquid. Filtration: separating an insoluble solid with a filter. Evaporation and distillation use differences in boiling point.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.4.3 Separation of mixtures – Sedimentation and Decantation · p.28
17666: Electrons in an ion = Z − charge. Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons (e.g. Ar, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻, S²⁻ all have 18). Valence electrons are the outer-shell electrons; nonmetals gain 8 − (valence electrons) electrons to form anions, e.g. N (5 valence e⁻) forms N³⁻ in Na₃N. Anions are larger than their atoms; cations smaller.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.2 Chemical Bonding – ionic bonding · p.60-65
17667: Isotopes have the same Z but different numbers of neutrons. Average atomic mass = Σ(fractional abundance × isotopic mass); it lies closer to the most abundant isotope (e.g. Cu ≈ 63.55 u).
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.1.4 Isotopes / Average atomic mass · p.48-49
17668: Metal + nonmetal → ionic (e.g. RbCl, K₂O). Nonmetal + nonmetal → covalent. Coordinate covalent bond: both shared electrons come from one atom (e.g. NH₄⁺).
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.2 Chemical Bonding – ionic bonding · p.60-65
17669: Identical atoms share electrons equally (H₂, Cl₂, O₂: nonpolar). Different nonmetals share unequally and the more electronegative atom becomes δ− (HCl, H₂O, HF: polar).
Textbook: Grade 10 · 2.2.3 Polar and Nonpolar Covalent Bonds · p.45-46
17670: Nonpolar molecules attract by dispersion forces; polar molecules (HCl) by dipole–dipole forces; polar + nonpolar by dipole–induced dipole forces. Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole–dipole attraction when H is bonded to F, O or N (HF, H₂O, NH₃). Molecular crystals held by these weak forces have low melting points.
17671: Criss-cross the charges and use brackets when more than one polyatomic ion is needed: Al³⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → Al₂(SO₄)₃; Ca²⁺ + PO₄³⁻ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 3.2.1 Chemical Formulas for Compounds (polyatomic ions) · p.93-94
17672: n = m/M. Number of molecules = n × 6.02×10²³; number of atoms = molecules × atoms per molecule (include water of crystallization, e.g. ZnSO₄·7H₂O has 27 atoms). For equal masses, the substance with the smallest molar mass has the most molecules.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 3.3.1 Mole / converting mass to particles · p.112-116
17673: Balance first, then use coefficients as mole ratios, e.g. 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O: 1 mol C₂H₂ gives 2 mol CO₂ (88 g).
17674: Balance atoms other than H and O first; for redox reactions make electrons lost = electrons gained (oxidation-number method), then balance O with H₂O and finally H.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.1.4 Writing and Balancing Simple Redox Equations · p.33-36
17675: The group of a main-group element equals its number of valence electrons. Alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb…) have 1 valence electron, form M⁺ ions and react with water: 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂ (solution becomes basic).
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.2 Chemical Bonding – ionic bonding · p.60-65
17676: Nuclear charge increases across a period while shielding stays similar, so electrons are held more tightly: radius ↓, IE ↑, EN ↑. Down a group, new shells are added: radius ↑, IE ↓, metallic character ↑.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.2 Chemical Bonding – formation of ions · p.62-64
17677: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom. It depends on distance from the nucleus, nuclear charge, shielding by inner shells and the type of electron. Removing an electron from a noble-gas core (e.g. Na⁺ → Na²⁺) needs a very large energy; He has the highest first IE.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.4.2 Trends in Ionization Energy · p.28-29
17678: A saturated solution contains the maximum dissolved solute at that temperature. Solubility is usually given in g per 100 g (or 100 mL) of water at a stated temperature.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.3.3 Colligative Properties – freezing point depression · p.105-106
17679: When a saturated solution is cooled, the mass of crystals formed = solubility at the higher temperature − solubility at the lower temperature (per 100 g water).
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.1.3 Solubility and the Solubility Curve · p.69-72
17680: Molarity M = moles of solute / litres of solution. Normality N = equivalents / litres = M × n, where n = replaceable H⁺ (acids) or OH⁻ (bases). Equivalent mass = molar mass / n (e.g. H₂SO₄ 49 g, Na₂CO₃ 53 g). Titration: MaVa·na = MbVb·nb.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 4.3.1–4.3.2 Titration / Determining concentration using titration · p.133-136
17681: Adding solute lowers the vapour pressure and freezing point and raises the boiling point and osmotic pressure. ΔTf = Kf·m (multiply by the number of ions for ionic solutes, e.g. MgCl₂ → 3 particles). Water: Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol, Kb = 0.52 °C·kg/mol.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.3.3 Colligative Properties – freezing point depression · p.105-106
17682: Monoprotic: HCl, HNO₃, CH₃COOH (only the –COOH H is acidic). Diprotic: H₂SO₄, H₂CO₃, H₂S. Triprotic: H₃PO₄. Acidic soil is treated with lime/limestone (CaCO₃); basic soil with ammonium sulphate.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 4.2.3 Preparation of bases – active metal + water · p.127
17683: [H₃O⁺] = 1×10⁻¹⁴/[OH⁻]. For strong bases count all OH⁻: 0.05 M Ba(OH)₂ → [OH⁻] = 0.10 M → pOH 1 → pH 13.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 4.5 The pH Scale (ionization of water) · p.144-145
17684: In titration a standard solution is added from a burette until the indicator changes colour (end point). Indicators are weak acids/bases that change colour by gaining/losing H⁺: phenolphthalein colourless (acid)/pink (base); methyl orange pink/yellow; litmus red/blue.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 4.3.1–4.3.2 Titration / Determining concentration using titration · p.133-136
17685: All nitrates and all Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ salts are soluble. Only Na, K and NH₄ carbonates are soluble. AgCl and PbSO₄, BaSO₄ are insoluble; CaSO₄ is only slightly soluble.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 4.4.3 General Properties of Salts – Table 4.4 Solubility of salts · p.141
17686: Balance the equation first; the heat value belongs to the mole amounts in the balanced equation. Heat for x mol = (x / coefficient) × ΔH. Heat of fusion: heat to melt 1 mol of solid at its melting point; heat of vaporization: 1 mol liquid → vapour at its boiling point.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 5.2.5 Heat of Fusion · p.176
17687: Activation energy is the minimum collision energy needed for reaction. Higher temperature increases the rate of ALL reactions (exothermic or endothermic). Smaller particles = larger surface area = faster. Catalysts lower the activation energy; inhibitors slow reactions.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.1.2 The Collision Theory of Reaction Rates · p.6-7
17688: If a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, it shifts to relieve the stress. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction (reverse for exothermic reactions); increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.2.2 Le Chatelier's Principle · p.22-23
17689: Rules: element = 0; O = −2; H = +1 (with nonmetals); group 1 = +1; sum = charge. Example: S in NaHSO₄ = +6. In 2HNO₃ + 3SO₂ + 2H₂O → 3H₂SO₄ + 2NO, HNO₃ (N +5 → +2) is the oxidizing agent and SO₂ (S +4 → +6) the reducing agent.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.1.4 Writing and Balancing Simple Redox Equations · p.33-36
17690: Electrolysis: decomposition of an electrolyte by electric current. Which ion is discharged depends on (1) position in the electrochemical series, (2) concentration and (3) nature of the electrodes. Cathode: reduction; anode: oxidation.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.2.1 What is Electrolysis? · p.38
17691: Q = I × t. Mass deposited m = (A/(Z·F)) × I × t, with F = 96 500 C/mol and Z = electrons per ion (Cu²⁺: Z = 2).
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.2.6 Faraday's Law of Electrolysis · p.59-63
17692: Sulphur occurs free in underground deposits and is extracted by the Frasch process; it has rhombic and monoclinic allotropes. Ammonia is a colourless, pungent, very soluble basic gas.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.3.2 Ammonia – Industrial preparation (Haber process) · p.90-91
17693: Haber → NH₃; Ostwald → HNO₃; Contact → H₂SO₄; Frasch → S.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.3.2 Ammonia – Industrial preparation (Haber process) · p.90-91
17694: Roasting: heating a sulphide ore in excess air → oxide + SO₂. Calcination: heating a carbonate ore in limited air → oxide + CO₂. The oxide is then reduced, e.g. ZnO + C → Zn + CO.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 4.1.3 Activity series and metallurgy – Table 4.2 Common metal ores · p.124
17695: Convert °C to K (+273) and mL to L. Molar mass from STP data: M = d × 22.4 or M = m × 22.4 / V(L). At constant T, expansion lowers the pressure; average kinetic energy depends only on temperature.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 5.2.3 Avogadro's Law (molar volume at STP) · p.172-175
17696: Postulates: tiny particles with negligible volume; constant random straight-line motion; perfectly elastic collisions; no intermolecular forces; average kinetic energy ∝ absolute temperature. Real gases deviate at low T and high P.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 5.3 The Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases · p.183-186
17697: 2 pairs linear (CO₂); 3 bonding pairs trigonal planar (BF₃, AlCl₃, each C in C₂H₄); 4 bonding pairs tetrahedral (CH₄); 3 bonding + 1 lone pair trigonal pyramidal (NH₃, 107°); 2 bonding + 2 lone pairs bent (H₂O). A double bond counts as one pair.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.1 Shapes of simple molecules – ammonia · p.10
17698: Cubic a = b = c, all 90°; tetragonal a = b ≠ c, all 90°; orthorhombic a ≠ b ≠ c, all 90°; triclinic a ≠ b ≠ c and α ≠ β ≠ γ ≠ 90°. Molecular crystals (ice, solid Ne) have the lowest melting points; covalent network crystals (diamond) the highest.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.2.3 Types of Crystals · p.17-18
17699: Organic compounds are carbon compounds classified by carbon skeleton and functional group.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.3.5 Organic Polymers – addition polymerization, Table of thermoplastics · p.92-96
17700: A carbon bonded to 1, 2, 3 or 4 other carbons is primary, secondary, tertiary or quaternary (3-methylpentane has a tertiary carbon). Complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.2.1 Hydrocarbons – saturated and unsaturated · p.34-35
17701: CH₂O (methanal) is the simplest aldehyde; CH₃COCH₃ is a ketone.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.3.3 Other derivatives – Aldehydes and Ketones · p.82-83
17702: Primary alcohols oxidize to aldehydes then carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols to ketones; tertiary alcohols resist oxidation. Alcohols react with Na to give alkoxides + H₂.
17703: IUPAC names: alkane −e + oic acid (HCOOH methanoic acid = formic acid; CH₃COOH ethanoic acid = acetic acid). Acids react with active metals to give salts + H₂: 2CH₃CH₂COOH + 2Na → 2CH₃CH₂COONa (sodium propanoate) + H₂.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.3.2 Carboxylic Acids – naming · p.79
17704: Ester RCOOR′ is named alkyl (R′) + acid-oate: CH₃(CH₂)₄COOCH₂CH₃ = ethyl hexanoate. Amides: alkane −e + amide, carbonyl carbon = C1: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CONH₂ = 3-methylbutanamide.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.3.3 Other Derivatives – Esters and Amides (naming) · p.84-85
17705: Find the longest chain containing the functional group, number from the end nearest the functional group, name branches with position numbers.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.3.2 Carboxylic Acids – naming · p.79
17706: Isomers have the same molecular formula (and molar mass) but different structures: the butanols C₄H₁₀O all have M = 74 g/mol, whereas butanal C₄H₈O has 72 g/mol.
17707: Addition polymers form from alkenes (polythene, PVC from vinyl chloride, polystyrene, Teflon from CF₂=CF₂) – thermoplastics. Condensation polymers eliminate small molecules (nylon, polyester, Bakelite, urea–methanal). Thermosetting plastics are heat resistant and cannot be remoulded.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.3.5 Organic Polymers – addition polymerization, Table of thermoplastics · p.92-96
17708: Saponification: fat + NaOH → soap + glycerol. Salting out: adding concentrated NaCl makes the soap separate as curds from the glycerol solution.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.3.4 Soaps and Detergents – preparation of soap · p.86-87
17709: Remaining mass = initial × (1/2)ⁿ, n = time/half-life (same time units). Nuclear equations must balance mass numbers and atomic numbers, e.g. ²³⁹₉₂U + ⁴₂He → ²⁴²₉₄Pu + ¹₀n (transmutation of U to Pu).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.2 Radioactive Decay Rates (Half-life); Table 3.4 · p.118-121
17710: Mass defect Δm = mass of products − mass of reactants (negative: mass lost). Energy ΔE = Δm c², with Δm in kg and c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s gives joules. For p + n → ²H (masses in the exam) Δm = −7.5×10⁻³⁰ kg, E = 6.75×10⁻¹³ J.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.3.1 The Power of the Nucleus – ΔE = Δmc², mass defect of deuterium · p.121-122
17711: Agriculture is treated as an industry (G12 4.1.3). It supplies raw materials to food-processing, textile, leather, brewery and sugar industries (G11 1.2.4). Livestock plough land, provide manure, food, income and employment (G12 1.1.3).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 4.1.3 Agriculture as Industry · p.212
17712: Sedentary agro-pastoralism (mixed farming) ≈ 67 % of farmers – dominant. Nomadic pastoralism prevails in the semi-desert zone. Semi-nomadic pastoralism (transhumance) occurs in spate-irrigation areas such as Sheeb.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.3 Farming Systems in Eritrea · p.9-11
17713: Plant sciences: agronomy, horticulture, plant breeding and protection. Animal sciences: nutrition, breeding, aquaculture, etc. Veterinary science is listed under production support and management.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.5 Branches of Agricultural Sciences · p.29-33
17714: Yield-defining factors (CO₂, solar radiation, temperature, humidity, crop physiology, altitude, latitude, crop/breed type) cannot be changed much; yield-limiting factors (water, N, P, K) can be supplied; yield-reducing factors are weeds, pests and diseases.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.4 Constraints on Agricultural Development · p.18
17715: Isotherms join places of equal mean temperature. Instruments: rain gauge (rainfall), barometer/barograph (pressure), sunshine recorder (sunshine hours/intensity), radiometer (radiation), thermo-hygrograph (temperature and humidity), anemometer (wind).
17716: Five roles of soil: plant growth, habitat for organisms, nutrient recycling, water supply and purification, engineering medium. Soil-forming factors: parent material, climate, biota, topography and time. Profile: O (litter), A (humus-rich topsoil), B (subsoil, illuviation), C (weathered parent material), R (bedrock).
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.2 Soil (five major ecological roles of soil, Figure 2.2) · p.45
17717: Bulk density = dry mass/total volume; particle density = dry mass/volume of solids; porosity = pore volume/total volume; water content = (W1 − W2)/W1 × 100. Physical properties: texture, structure, consistency. Chemical: pH, colloids, ion exchange, salinity; lime supplies Ca (and Mg from dolomite).
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.2.11 Chemical Properties of Soil – calcareous and dolomitic soils · p.66
17718: Ten themes include integrated management, sustainable use, management of alien invasive species, in-situ and ex-situ conservation.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.3.1 Terrestrial Biodiversity (10 themes) · p.76
17719: Setit (rises in central Ethiopia), Mereb-Gash (upper basin badly eroded), Barka-Anseba, Red Sea (flows used for spate irrigation and aquifer recharge) and Danakil (short runoff events).
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.4.3 The Major River Basins of Eritrea · p.88-90
17720: Six zones: moist highland, arid highland, moist lowland, arid lowland, sub-humid (700–1100 mm, 1 % of area) and semi-desert (< 200 mm, 39 % of area – largest and driest).
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.5.2 The Agro-ecological Zones of Eritrea (Table 2.13) · p.95
17721: Dicots: two cotyledons, flower parts in 4s or 5s, reticulate veins, tap root (beans, tomato, pumpkin); monocots: maize, sorghum, barley. Micronutrients: Mn, Fe, Mo, Cu, B, Zn, Cl. Long-day plants need > 12 h light (e.g. wheat); short-day < 12 h.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.1.1 Crops – monocots and dicots (Table 3.1) · p.102
17722: Forage crops are grown for feed (hay, silage, pasture). Catch (emergence) crops are quick-growing annuals sown after a crop failure. Cover, green-manure and companion crops have other purposes.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.2.2 The Classification of Field Crops · p.124
17723: Germination % = germinated/total × 100. Weeds compete with crops but also give feed, manure, medicine and building material. Resistant varieties are the cheapest and best insect control. Cultivation controls weeds, aerates soil and conserves moisture.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.3.6 Weeds, Insects and Diseases · p.138-139
17724: Mono-cropping, mixed cropping, intercropping, alley cropping, fallowing and crop rotation (different crops in sequence on the same land).
17725: Pomology – fruits; olericulture – vegetables; floriculture – flowers. Nurseries raise seedlings (peasant, standard, temporary). Seeds are easy to store, handle and sow by machine; vegetative propagation gives true-to-type plants.
17726: Perissodactyla (odd-toed): horses, donkeys. Even-toed: cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, camels. Poultry digestive tract: crop, proventriculus, gizzard, intestines, caeca, cloaca (no rumen). Goat: buck, doe, kid, wether.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.1.4 Types and Classification of Livestock · p.4
17727: Dry matter = feed − water. Concentrates (grains, brans, cakes) are high-energy, low-fibre; roughages (hay, straw, stover) are fibrous. Lipids give 2.25 × the energy of carbohydrates. Zero grazing = cut-and-carry.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.2.2 Common Classifications and Types of Feeds · p.24
17728: Beef breeds: Angus, Hereford, Simmental, Charolais, Limousin, Gelbvieh, Brahman, Shorthorn. Dairy: Holstein-Friesian, Jersey, Guernsey, Brown Swiss, Ayrshire. Genetic improvement by selection, cross-breeding and artificial insemination; feeding, housing and disease control improve the environment.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.3 Routine Management Practices – dairy breeds and milk fat · p.30-31
17729: Culling, dehorning, castration, docking, shearing, hoof trimming and identification (tattooing, tagging, ear-notching, branding).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.3 Routine Management Practices – j) Methods used to identify livestock · p.47
17730: Good houses: warm, well drained, ventilated, easy to clean, non-slippery floor. Dairy: tail-to-tail (easy milking, cleaning, supervision, less disease) vs head-to-head (easy feeding, narrow barns). Gags keep the jaws apart for oral dosing.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.4 Animal Housing and Equipment · p.48-52
17731: TB is spread by raw milk and undercooked meat; controlled by hygiene, avoiding overcrowding, test-and-isolate. Ectoparasites (ticks, fleas, lice, flies, mites) live on the skin; endoparasites (roundworms, tapeworms, flukes) inside.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.5.1 Common Diseases – tuberculosis, brucellosis · p.63-64
17732: Tangible uses include wood products (timber, poles, firewood, charcoal) and non-wood products (gums, resins, incense, fruits, honey, medicine).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.2.3 The Role of Forests – b) Tangible uses · p.103-104
17733: Anthropogenic causes: farm expansion, wood extraction, overgrazing, non-wood over-extraction, war. Bare-root seedlings are cheap, light and simple to raise but their roots dry out; potted seedlings survive better on difficult sites.
17734: Protected areas (usually steep, degraded slopes) where grazing and cutting are restricted so vegetation regenerates; they reduce erosion and siltation, conserve flora and fauna and reserve pasture.
17735: Roles: food, science, aesthetics/heritage, tourism. Causes of decline: habitat destruction, drought, illegal trade, hunting, war, alien species, cultural beliefs. Conflict analysed with DPSIR. Challenges: poverty, beliefs, ownership and responsibility.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.3.1 The Role of Wildlife · p.127-128
17736: Proclamation 155/2006: forestry and wildlife; Proclamation 156/2006: plant quarantine. Protected areas: Gash-Setit (elephants), Semenawi Bahri (forest), Buri Peninsula (wild ass), Yob and Nakfa (Nubian ibex).
17737: Physical (structure deterioration), chemical (nutrient loss, salinity) and biological degradation. Speed and extent depend on soil type, relief, climate and intensity of land use. Major soil problems: acidity, salinity, alkalinity, compaction, erosion, swelling/shrinking clays.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.1.2 The Importance of Soil and Water Conservation · p.159-161
17738: Water erosion: splash (raindrop), sheet, rill, gully. Wind erosion: deflation, abrasion. Ice erosion: glacial, freeze–thaw.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.2.3 Soil Erosion – b) Water erosion · p.171-172
17739: Physical: terraces, stone bunds, diversion ditches, waterways, gully control. Biological/agronomic: afforestation, enclosures, grass strips, crop rotation, intercropping, tillage. Slope % = VI/HI × 100.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.3 Soil and Water Conservation Measures (Table 3.2) · p.176-177
17740: Dams store water for people, animals, irrigation and hydropower. Drip irrigation is the most water-efficient; sprinklers ≈ 75 %; furrow/basin 40–50 %.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.5.3 Methods of Irrigation · p.200
17741: Poor drainage: heavy rain, clay soils, sand over impermeable clay, hardpans. Advantages of drainage: aeration, deeper root zone, warmer soil and better nutrient uptake, more micro-organism activity, salinity control.
17742: The manager plans and coordinates activities, buys inputs, keeps records and pays wages.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 4.1.2 The Importance of Farm Management · p.210-211
17743: Factors: land, labour, capital, management, entrepreneurship. APP = TPP/X; MPP = ΔTPP/ΔX; MVP = MPP × output price; profit-maximizing input level where MVP = input price. Fixed costs (insurance, depreciation, housing) vs variable costs (fuel, repairs). Rainfall is uncontrollable.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 4.1.5 Basic Economic Principles – costs · p.222-223
17744: Petty cash book (only cash transactions), wage book, inventory. Depreciation = (CP − SV)/E; book value = CP − accumulated depreciation. Balance sheet = financial position on a date; income statement = period.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 4.2.3 Financial Statements – balance sheet · p.239-240
17745: Co-operatives have an economic purpose, are member-owned and controlled, run for members, not charities or state-directed. Principles: voluntary and open membership, democratic control, economic participation, autonomy, education, cooperation, concern for community.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 4.4.2 Types of CBO – c) Co-operative principles · p.253-254
17746: Traditional poultry scavenge, get leftovers and night shelter; indigenous birds are hardy but lay small eggs. Bee castes: queen, workers (build hive, collect nectar, make wax/honey, feed young, defend) and drones (only mate with virgin queens). Beekeeping needs little capital and land, suits both sexes of any age and can be a secondary activity.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.3 Poultry production systems · p.39
17747: Textbook 2.4.3: wind, solar and geothermal are renewable alternatives; kerosene, LPG, rural electrification and improved stoves reduce the demand for fuel wood. Wind power is clean and renewable but intermittent.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.4.3 Alternative Energy Sources · p.146-148
17748: Investment capital buys irrigation systems, buildings, tractors; working capital meets day-to-day costs (seed, fertilizer, fuel, wages). Net revenue = total revenue − total cost. A partial budget assesses minor changes in the farm plan; a complete budget the whole farm. Depreciation (straight line) = (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 4.2 Farm Accounting – types of capital · p.236
17749: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, plastids (chloroplasts) and a large central vacuole. The Grade 9 textbook lists centrioles and lysosomes as found only in animal cells. Ribosomes occur in all cells; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, prokaryotes (bacteria) do not.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.2.2 The Cell Structure – plant cell organelles · p.14-15
17750: Diffusion and osmosis are passive (no energy, down a concentration gradient; osmosis = water through a selectively permeable membrane). Active transport moves molecules into or out of the cell with the help of energy (ATP), even against a concentration gradient.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.3.2 The Transportation of Molecules · p.19
17751: Bacterial diseases: gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae), syphilis (Treponema pallidum), tetanus, pneumonia, tuberculosis, salmonellosis, anthrax. Viral diseases: smallpox, common cold, chickenpox, influenza, herpes, polio, rabies, Ebola, HIV/AIDS. Some bacteria (E. coli) exchange genetic material by conjugation, a primitive sexual reproduction.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.5.3 Diseases Caused by Viruses · p.42
17752: Euglena: flagellum at the anterior end attached at the base of the flask-shaped reservoir; contractile vacuole near the reservoir; gullet; numerous chloroplasts; light-sensitive eyespot (stigma); no cell wall but a flexible pellicle; nucleus. It reproduces by binary fission and forms cysts in bad conditions.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.3.2 Kingdom Protista – simple algae: Euglena · p.71-72
17753: Flatworms are acoelomate, roundworms (nematodes) pseudocoelomate, annelids and higher animals coelomate. Insects show metamorphosis: incomplete (egg → nymph → adult, grasshopper) or complete (egg → larva → pupa → adult, butterfly, housefly). Chondrichthyes (sharks, rays) have a cartilage skeleton, true jaws, two pairs of fins and a two-chambered heart.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.3.5 Kingdom Animalia – Arthropods (insects) · p.101
17754: Saturated fats (animal fats, solid at room temperature) have more hydrogen atoms than unsaturated fats (plant oils, liquid).
17755: Lack of protein → kwashiorkor; lack of energy foods → marasmus; lack of vitamin D → rickets. Fats need bile for emulsification before digestion.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.2.6 The Small Intestine – intestinal enzymes · p.38-40
17756: Dental formula = teeth on one side of upper/lower jaw; total = sum × 2 (dog i 3/3 c 1/1 pm 4/4 m 2/3 = 42; human 32). During swallowing the soft palate closes the nasal cavity and the epiglottis closes the trachea. Sucrase (invertase) digests sucrose → glucose + fructose. Bile from the liver is stored in the gall bladder and emulsifies fats.
17757: The human heart has two atria and two ventricles. AV valves (tricuspid, bicuspid) close at the start of ventricular contraction ('lub'); semilunar valves close afterwards ('dub'). Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; veins have valves and are helped by skeletal-muscle contraction.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 2.1.1 The Human Heart · p.51
17758: An Rh-negative person given Rh-positive blood makes anti-Rh antibodies; a second Rh-positive transfusion causes agglutination. Similar sensitisation causes Rh disease in a second Rh-positive pregnancy.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 2.5 Blood Types – the Rh blood group · p.79-80
17759: The lymphatic system is one-way (tissues → veins) with no pump; lymph is moved by skeletal muscles, breathing and smooth muscle. Lymph nodes are bean-shaped organs containing many leukocytes.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.2 Comparison between the Lymphatic System and the Circulatory System · p.95-96
17760: Active immunity: own antibodies (natural after infection, artificial after vaccination). Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies (natural – mother to baby via placenta/milk; artificial – serum or anti-venom injection); immediate but short-lived.
17761: The larynx (voice box) is an airway and produces sound: vocal cords vibrate as exhaled air passes. Inhalation: diaphragm contracts (pulls down), ribs move up and out, lungs expand. Exhalation: diaphragm relaxes to its dome shape.
17762: Skin excretes sweat (water, salts, urea), lungs CO₂ and water, liver bile pigments and urea formation, kidneys urine. Kidney failure is treated with an artificial kidney (dialysis, short-term) or kidney transplant (long-term).
Textbook: Grade 10 · 6.2 The Excretory Organs – kidney failure · p.137
17763: Internal receptors detect muscle length and tension, limb position, pain, blood composition, volume and pressure, body temperature. Deafness: calcified/pierced eardrum, excessive noise, blows on the cheek, pointed objects in the canal, fused ossicles.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 7.2 The Internal Receptors · p.159
17764: Cerebral lobes: frontal (voluntary movement), parietal (sensation), temporal (hearing, smell, memory), occipital (vision). Hypothalamus: temperature, blood pressure, water balance, appetite, emotions, pituitary control. Threshold = minimum stimulus that starts an impulse. A reflex is an automatic, involuntary response via a reflex arc through the spinal cord.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 8.2.1 The Central Nervous System – hypothalamus · p.174-175
17765: Hormones are proteins, steroids or amino-acid derivatives. Pituitary: GH, TSH, ACTH, prolactin (milk production), FSH, LH; posterior lobe releases ADH (water balance) and oxytocin (uterine contraction, milk release). Pancreas: beta cells → insulin, alpha cells → glucagon.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.1.4 The Adrenal Glands – steroid hormones · p.9-10
17766: Insulin lowers and glucagon raises blood glucose. The skin regulates temperature by sweating and changes in blood flow.
17767: Secondary sexual characteristics in both sexes: growth spurt, pubic and armpit hair; males: deeper voice, facial hair. Seminal vesicle: alkaline fluid with prostaglandins; Cowper's gland: lubricating mucus. Progesterone maintains the uterine lining. Umbilical vein carries food and O₂ to the fetus; umbilical arteries carry wastes away.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.1 Primary and Secondary Sexual Characteristics · p.26-27
17768: Bone layers: periosteum (smooth double-layered covering), compact bone, spongy bone. Axial skeleton: skull, vertebral column, sternum, ribs; appendicular: limbs and girdles.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.1.1 Structure and Composition of Bone · p.54
17769: Smooth muscle lines hollow organs, blood vessels, eyes, glands and skin; cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.
17770: The radicle emerges first, then the plumule. IAA is the natural auxin made in the shoot apical meristem; NAA and 2,4-D are synthetic auxins; cytokinins and ABA are other hormone classes.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 6.1.2 Seed Dormancy and Germination · p.106
17771: Upper and lower epidermis are separated by the mesophyll (palisade + spongy layers); the waxy cuticle covers the epidermis.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 6.4.2 The Leaf: Structure and Function · p.126-127
17772: One male nucleus fuses with the egg (zygote); the second fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the endosperm – double fertilization, found only in flowering plants.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 6.4.3 The Flower: Structure and Function · p.130
17773: RNA has uracil instead of thymine. Transcription pairs DNA A→U, T→A, G→C, C→G (ATGCA → UACGU).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.1.3 Protein Synthesis – transcription · p.10-11
17774: Mitosis: prophase (chromosomes shorten and thicken), metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Meiosis produces haploid (monoploid) gametes.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.2.2 Meiosis and Sexual Reproduction · p.18
17775: Mendel chose peas: quick maturity, controllable pollination, fertile seeds after crossing, contrasting characters. A test cross with the homozygous recessive shows whether a dominant individual is homozygous or heterozygous; Ff × ff gives 1 : 1.
17776: Sex-linked genes are on sex chromosomes, mostly X. X-linked recessive traits (colour blindness, haemophilia) affect mostly males; a colour-blind daughter needs a colour-blind father and a carrier or colour-blind mother.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.4.2 Sex-Linked Characters – colour blindness · p.46-47
17777: Evolution changes populations, not individuals. Homologous organs indicate a common ancestor; greater similarity means closer relationship.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.1 Theories of Evolution · p.60
17778: Cold: fur, fat, higher metabolism, shivering, hibernation, small ears. Heat: large ears, no fat layer (camel), evaporative cooling. Salt: mangroves. Dry: cactus.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 4.3.1 Adaptations of Animals to Low Temperatures · p.150
17779: A food chain is a single linear sequence of energy flow; a food web is many interconnected food chains, more complex and more stable.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.3 Food Relationships – food chains and food webs · p.101-103
17780: Tropical rain forests (equatorial belt, warm and wet all year) harbour more species than any other terrestrial biome; tundra and taiga are cold with low diversity.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.5 Biomes of the World – tropical rain forest · p.116
17781: Cell theory: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the smallest unit of life; cells come from pre-existing cells. Microscope: the revolving nose piece rotates the objective lenses into position.
17782: Living things are made of cells, grow and develop, reproduce, respond to stimuli, respire/use energy (metabolism), excrete, move, and maintain homeostasis.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.1 Characteristics of living things · p.1
17783: Unicellular prokaryotes; shapes rods (bacilli), spheres (cocci) and spirals (spirilla); cell walls of peptidoglycan (not chitin); autotrophic (photosynthetic/chemosynthetic) or heterotrophic (saprophytes, parasites). Cyanobacteria with red pigment periodically colour the Red Sea; they reproduce by cell division or fragmentation.
17784: Euglena, Entamoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium, Chlamydomonas and Spirogyra are protists. Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga with spiral chloroplasts; it reproduces by simple cell division (fission) and, in unfavourable conditions, by conjugation.
17785: Fungi have chitin cell walls. Yeasts ferment sugar for bread, beer and wine and reproduce by budding; Penicillium gives the antibiotic penicillin; some fungi are pathogens.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.5 Fungi – economic importance · p.78-81
17786: A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals and water (plus fibre). Fat leaves a translucent spot on paper. Carbohydrates contain C, H, O with H : O = 2 : 1; monosaccharides (CH₂O)ₙ, e.g. C₆H₁₂O₆. Polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) are not sweet and insoluble. Too much saturated fat → atherosclerosis.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.1 Food and nutrients – balanced diet · p.1
17787: Aerobic respiration: glucose + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy (the main respiratory wastes). Anaerobic respiration in yeast = alcoholic fermentation (glucose → ethanol + CO₂) used for bread, beer, wine, 'mies' and 'suwa'; in muscle it gives lactic acid.
17788: Blood path: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. Systemic circulation is the largest circuit. Arteries: thick walls, no valves (except at their origin); veins: thin walls with valves; capillaries: walls one cell thick, no valves.
17789: Group O has anti-A and anti-B antibodies in the plasma; AB has none. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant, i recessive: a child can be AB only if one parent supplies Iᴬ and the other Iᴮ.
17790: Lymph moves through lymphatic vessels mainly by muscular activity (contraction of skeletal muscles squeezing the vessels), with valves preventing backflow. Lymphatic tissue contains lymphocytes and macrophages (not erythrocytes). Antigens are macromolecules that trigger an immune response.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.1 Lymph and lymphatic tissue · p.87
17791: External respiration = exchange of O₂ and CO₂ between the alveoli (lungs) and blood. Inhalation: diaphragm contracts and flattens, intercostal muscles raise ribs and sternum, thorax volume increases. Exhalation: diaphragm relaxes (domes up), ribs return, thorax volume decreases.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 5.1 Respiration – external and internal · p.108
17792: Hormones are secretions of ductless endocrine glands, carried by blood (proteins, amines or steroids); enzymes are proteins secreted mainly by exocrine glands through ducts. Pituitary disorders: gigantism, dwarfism, acromegaly, diabetes insipidus (ADH); goitre is thyroid. Calcium is regulated by parathyroid hormone and calcitonin (thyroid). LH from the pituitary stimulates testosterone and progesterone. Drinking much water lowers ADH secretion.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.2 Pituitary gland – disorders · p.3-5
17793: Sexual reproduction involves fusion of gametes (two parents, variation); asexual reproduction involves one parent and no gametes (identical offspring). Somatic cells form by mitosis, gametes by meiosis (haploid: 48 → 24). The umbilical cord joins embryo and placenta: its vein brings food and oxygenated blood, its arteries take deoxygenated blood and wastes.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.3 Cyanobacteria – mode of reproduction · p.66
17794: Endoskeleton: internal, grows smoothly without moulting, supports great size and weight. The human skeletal system = cartilages, ligaments and 206 bones; bones store minerals and fat, contain blood vessels, nerves and bone cells. Ligaments join bone to bone. Pivot joint (atlas–axis) turns the head. Skull = cranium + facial bones + ear ossicles; appendicular skeleton = limbs and girdles. Smooth muscle lines stomach, intestine, bladder and uterus; the heart is cardiac muscle. Muscles produce the force for movement.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 4.1 Types of muscles · p.78-79
17795: Hydrophytes live in water or waterlogged conditions. Succulents: leaves reduced to spines, green photosynthetic stem, water-storing stem, few sunken waxy stomata. Animals in cold: hormonal changes raising metabolic rate, insulation, hibernation, small ears.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 4.2 Adaptations of plants to water – xerophytes/succulents · p.145-146
17796: DNA is a ladder: sugar–phosphate backbones are the sides, paired nitrogenous bases the steps. mRNA is transcribed from a DNA template. Gene mutations: substitution, deletion, insertion, inversion (a segment rotated through 180°).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.5 Mutation – gene mutations · p.50-51
17797: Homozygous: two identical alleles (TT, tt); heterozygous: two different alleles (Tt).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.4 Mendelian genetics – terms · p.31
17798: Adaptation enables organisms to survive in a particular environment. Branches: botany, zoology, ecology, cytology, evolution; the study of parasites is parasitology.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.1.1 What is biology? – characteristics of living things · p.1-2
17799: Objective lens: brings the image into focus and magnifies it; eyepiece (ocular): magnifies; coarse/fine adjustment knobs focus; diaphragm controls light.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.1.3 The microscope – parts and functions · p.7
17800: Kingdom → phylum → class → order → family → genus → species. Scientific name = Genus + species (Equus caballus). Monera: prokaryotes; Protista: mostly unicellular/simple; Fungi: eukaryotes with extracellular digestion; Plantae: multicellular, cell walls, photosynthetic; Animalia: multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.1 The importance of classification – levels of classification · p.54
17801: Prokaryotes with cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid, pili and flagella. Diseases: tuberculosis, gonorrhoea, syphilis, anthrax, cholera (rabies is viral). Rhizobium in legume root nodules fixes nitrogen.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.4.1 The structures and forms of bacteria · p.28-30
17802: Cnidarians: radial symmetry, tentacles with stinging cells, two tissue layers. Dicot leaves have net (reticulate) venation; monocots parallel venation. Plant life cycles alternate between sporophyte and gametophyte generations.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 6.4.2 The leaf: structure and function (venation) · p.125
17803: Carbohydrates contain C, H and O only. Fats are saturated or unsaturated according to the number of hydrogen atoms in their fatty acids. Marasmus: protein–energy deficiency. Magnesium deficiency: muscle weakness and cramps.
17804: Mechanical (physical) digestion: taking in, moistening (lubrication), chewing, peristalsis. Chemical digestion: enzymatic hydrolysis. Absorption: nutrients pass from the intestine into the blood (fats into lacteals). Pancreas makes enzymes, liver makes bile, gall bladder stores bile.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.3 Digestion – mechanical and chemical digestion · p.22, 26
17805: Light reaction converts light energy into chemical energy; chlorophyll absorbs light. The dark reaction (light-independent) makes sugar from CO₂. Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 3.2 Photosynthesis – light and dark reactions · p.128-129
17806: The heart (size of a closed fist) lies in the thoracic cavity between the lungs; it is a double pump. Pericardial fluid between pericardium and heart reduces friction. Superior vena cava returns blood from the upper body, inferior vena cava from the lower body, to the right atrium.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 2.1.1 The human heart – location · p.49
17807: Tonsils trap bacteria entering the throat. Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes (B cells) against antigens. The immune system defends the body against microbes, toxins and parasites.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 4.2 Specific immunity – antibodies · p.99-101
17808: Main metabolic wastes in mammals: CO₂, excess water, salts, urea and red (bile) pigments. The loop of Henle lies in the medulla of the kidney.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 6.1 The excretory products · p.126-127
17809: Prolactin stimulates milk production (oxytocin causes milk ejection). The thyroid is the largest endocrine gland and is critical to development and maturation. LH stimulates interstitial cells to release androgens. Hypoglycaemia = low blood sugar.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.1.1 The pituitary gland – prolactin · p.3-4
17810: Cartilage is converted to bone by ossification. Axial skeleton: skull, vertebral column, thorax (ribs, sternum); appendicular: limbs and girdles. Humerus = upper arm; femur = thigh.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.1 Cartilage and bone – ossification · p.54, 57
17811: Smooth muscle: airways, gut, blood vessels, skin (not the heart – cardiac muscle). Skeletal muscles work in antagonistic pairs (flexor/extensor), have origin and insertion, and lift loads; peristalsis is done by smooth muscle.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 4.1 Types of muscles · p.74-75
17812: Simple tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; complex tissues: xylem and phloem. Shoot system: stem, leaves, buds, flowers, fruits and seeds.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 6.2 Plant tissues – simple and complex · p.112-114
17813: The radicle emerges first during germination. Plant hormones are chemicals that act on target tissues, help the plant respond to the environment and can stimulate or inhibit growth.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 6.1.2 Seed dormancy and germination · p.104-106
17814: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the DNA template (A→U, T→A, G→C, C→G). Protein synthesis in the cytoplasm needs mRNA, tRNA, rRNA/ribosomes – DNA stays in the nucleus. Meiosis produces gametes for sexual reproduction.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.1 Protein synthesis – transcription · p.10-12
17815: Monohybrid cross: F₁ all dominant; F₂ phenotypic 3 : 1, genotypic 1 : 2 : 1. Haemophilia is X-linked recessive: a normal mother with a haemophiliac son is a carrier XᴴXʰ. Genotype = genetic make-up.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.3 Mendel's monohybrid crosses · p.33-35
17816: Lamarck: use and disuse, inheritance of acquired characters. Darwin: over-production, variation, struggle for existence (competition), survival of the fittest, inheritance.
17817: A niche is an organism's role, including when it is active. Mutualism: both partners benefit. Bacteria and fungi decompose dead organisms and recycle nutrients.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.3.5 Mutualism (with 3.3.3 parasitism, 3.3.4 commensalism) · p.104-105
17818: Grasslands: low rainfall with shrubs and small trees; deserts: very low rainfall. The pyramid of biomass compares biomass at each trophic level and narrows sharply from producers to carnivores.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.5 Biomes of the world – grasslands · p.119
17819: Viruses have no cells (no nucleus, cytoplasm or membrane) and cannot metabolise or replicate outside a host cell. Lytic cycle: attachment → penetration (injection of nucleic acid) → replication/synthesis → assembly (maturation) → lysis (release).
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.5.2 Viruses – comparison with cells · p.41
17820: Homeostasis = maintenance of a constant internal environment. A constant body temperature keeps enzymes at their optimum. Water loss → hypothalamus detects concentrated blood → more ADH from posterior pituitary → more water reabsorbed in the nephrons → blood water rises. Exercise, balanced diet, sleep and rest help homeostasis.
17821: Complete flower: sepals, petals, stamens (anther + filament) and pistil (stigma, style, ovary). The embryo's radicle becomes the root and the plumule the shoot.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 7.1.4 Common eye defects · p.153
17822: Darwin: overproduction, variation, struggle for existence, survival of the fittest. Vestigial organs (human appendix) are reduced, generally useless organs – evidence from comparative anatomy.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.1 Evidence of evolution – comparative anatomy (vestigial organs) · p.72
17823: Genetic recombination (crossing over, independent assortment, fertilisation) creates new combinations; mutation creates new alleles. Isolating mechanisms: behavioural (courtship song), seasonal, habitat, mechanical, gametic/zygotic mortality.
17824: Trophic levels: producers, primary consumers (herbivores), secondary/tertiary consumers (carnivores) – decomposers recycle. Carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion/industry. Oxygen cycle: photosynthesis releases O₂; respiration uses O₂ and returns CO₂ and water.
17825: Intra-specific: co-operation, competition, division of territory, hierarchy. Inter-specific: predation (most significant), parasitism, competition between species. Acid rain comes from air pollution (SO₂ and nitrogen oxides from burning fuels).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.1 Ecosystem – intra- and inter-specific relations · p.89
17826: Fungi phyla: Zygomycota (filamentous, cottony, no cross walls – bread mould), Ascomycota (sac fungi, yeasts), Basidiomycota, Deuteromycota (imperfect fungi). Plants: bryophytes (seedless, non-vascular – mosses, liverworts), pteridophytes (seedless vascular – ferns), gymnosperms, angiosperms. Autotrophs include cyanobacteria, algae (e.g. Spirogyra) and green plants.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.3 The five-kingdom classification (autotroph defined) · p.61
17827: Sponges are asymmetrical; cnidarians (Hydra, jellyfish) are radially symmetrical; flatworms (Platyhelminthes) and higher animals are bilaterally symmetrical with cephalization.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.3.5 Kingdom Animalia – symmetry; Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes · p.87-91
17828: Syphilis (STD) – Treponema pallidum; tuberculosis – Mycobacterium tuberculosis; anthrax – Bacillus anthracis; typhoid – Salmonella.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.4.2 The economic importance of bacteria – syphilis · p.36
17829: Learned behaviour: habituation, imprinting (a young animal forms a strong attachment to an individual, usually a parent, in a limited period; irreversible), associative learning (classical, operant conditioning), exploratory learning and insight learning.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 8.3.2 Learned behaviour – imprinting · p.188-189
17830: Exocrine (duct) glands: sweat, salivary, tear glands; endocrine (ductless): pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas, thymus. Disorders: pituitary GH excess – gigantism; thyroid/iodine – goitre; adrenal cortex failure – Addison's disease; pancreas (insulin failure) – diabetes mellitus.
Textbook: Grade 11 · Unit 1 introduction and summary – exocrine and endocrine glands · p.1, 16
17831: Population: a group of organisms of the same species living in the same area; community: all populations in an area interacting; ecosystem: the community plus its non-living environment; niche: the role of a species; habitat: where it lives.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.1 What is ecology? – levels of organisation, habitat, niche · p.86-87
17832: Economics is the study of how individuals and societies choose to use their scarce resources to satisfy their material wants as much as possible. Resources are limited, wants are unlimited – this scarcity is the basic economic problem.
Textbook: Grade 10 · Unit 1 introduction – Scarcity, choice and the definition of economics · p.2
17833: The PPC shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all its resources and technology. Points on the curve are efficient, points inside are attainable but inefficient, points outside are unattainable. Moving along the curve shows opportunity cost.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.1.3 Production Possibilities Curve (PPC) · p.11-13
17834: Land (natural resources, reward rent), labour (human effort, wage), capital (man-made goods used to produce other goods, interest) and entrepreneurship (decision making and risk taking, profit).
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.1.1 Types of Factors of Production · p.10
17835: Free market (capitalist): private property, economic freedom, voluntary exchange, profit motive, competition; prices set by supply and demand. Command: public ownership, central planning. Mixed: features of both.
Textbook: Grade 10 · Unit 1 introduction – (ii) Economic Systems: capitalist/free market system · p.5-6
17836: Sole proprietorship, partnership (unlimited liability), corporation (separate legal entity, ownership in shares, limited liability, continuity, large capital, professional employees; disadvantages: double taxation, large initial cost, owner–manager conflict) and cooperatives.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.2 Business Organizations – C. Corporation · p.19
17837: Transport: road, railway, water, air, pipeline (liquids and gases such as petroleum), ropeway, human- and animal-powered. Modern communication systems: visual, acoustic (telephone, telegraph, record player), telecommunication and data-processing.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.3.2 Communication Systems – Acoustic Communication Systems · p.26-27
17838: Barter = exchange of goods for goods without money (needs double coincidence of wants). Functions of money: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payments. Metallic money: standard (full-bodied) coins – metal value = face value; token coins – face value > metal value.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 2.1.2 Forms of Money – Metallic money · p.37
17839: Central bank: issues currency, banker/agent/adviser to government, holds member banks' reserves, lender of last resort. Commercial banks accept deposits and grant loans. Eritrea: Bank of Eritrea, Commercial Bank, Housing and Commerce Bank, Eritrean Development and Investment Bank, and the Savings and Micro-Credit Program (loans to poor households and small businesses).
Textbook: Grade 10 · 2.2.1 Types of Banks – Functions of a Central Bank (National Bank) · p.45-46
17840: Characteristics: sharing (pooling) of losses, payment of accidental losses, risk transfer (possibility of loss moves from insured to insurer), indemnification. Legal principles: indemnity, insurable interest, subrogation (textbook: an individual should not claim compensation from two sources), utmost good faith, contribution.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 2.3.1 Basic Characteristics of Insurance – c. Risk Transfer · p.53
17841: Perfect competition: many buyers/sellers, homogeneous products, perfect information, perfect mobility, free entry/exit, horizontal firm demand curve. Monopoly: one seller, no close substitutes, fixes EITHER price OR quantity, downward-sloping demand. Monopolistic competition, oligopoly, duopoly. Buyer side: monopsony (one buyer), oligopsony (few buyers).
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.1.1 Market Structure – a) Monopoly · p.4-5
17842: Law of demand: price up → quantity demanded down. Exceptions: Giffen and Veblen goods (demand rises with price). Substitutes (sugar–honey) vs complements (car–gasoline). Normal goods: demand rises with income; inferior goods: demand falls as income rises.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.2 Demand and Supply – Exceptions to the law of demand: b) Veblen goods · p.11
17843: Ped = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP, computed from the ORIGINAL values: [(Q₂ − Q₁)/Q₁] ÷ [(P₂ − P₁)/P₁]; sign usually dropped. Ped > 1 elastic, = 1 unitary, < 1 inelastic, 0 perfectly inelastic, ∞ perfectly elastic. Income elasticity negative for inferior goods.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.3.1 Elasticity of Demand – c) Income elasticity of demand · p.30
17844: TC = TFC + TVC. Fixed costs do not change with output and must be paid even at zero output; variable costs change with output. For TC = a + bQ, TFC = a and TVC = bQ.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.4 Cost of Production – short-term fixed and variable costs · p.39-40
17845: Consumer equilibrium: MUA/PA = MUB/PB. A price fall → buy more → MU falls (diminishing MU), giving a downward-sloping demand curve. Indifference curves slope downward, are convex to the origin, higher curves = more satisfaction, and never intersect.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.5 Consumer Choice and Demand – consumer equilibrium and deriving the demand curve · p.48-50
17846: GDP/GNP, NNP = GNP − depreciation, NI = income of factors (wages, rent, interest, profit) / NNP − indirect business taxes, PI, disposable income Yd = PI − personal taxes, personal saving = Yd − C. Expenditure approach C + I + G + (X − M); consumption is the largest component. Per capita income = GDP or GNP ÷ population.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.1.1 Measuring National Economic Performance – Disposable Personal Income · p.6
17847: C = a + bYd → S = −a + (1 − b)Yd. MPC + MPS = 1. Net investment = gross investment − depreciation. Investment demand depends on the interest rate and the marginal efficiency of capital.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.2.3 Investment – Review exercise (net investment) · p.23
17848: Public finance studies how the government raises revenue and makes expenditure. Government intervenes because of public goods, externalities (costs/benefits to third parties) and inequality. Taxation is the major source of public revenue.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.3 Public Finance – Introduction (definition) · p.25
17849: Comparative advantage = lower opportunity cost. Terms of trade = Px/Pm. BOP: current account (goods and services), capital account (investments and loans), official reserve account. Exchange rate = price of one currency in terms of another.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.4.1 International Trade Theories – comparative advantage · p.38
17850: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Changes must balance: ΔA = ΔL + ΔC.
17851: Assets and expenses (and drawings) increase on the debit side; liabilities, capital and revenue increase on the credit side. Buying equipment for cash: Dr Equipment, Cr Cash. Owner's investment: Dr Cash, Cr Capital.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.2.1 Transaction Analysis – Transaction 2: Purchase of an asset for cash · p.84
17852: Chart of accounts = list of account titles and numbers showing their arrangement in the ledger. Posting transfers journal amounts to ledger accounts; the journal page number goes in the ledger's Post Ref. column and the account number in the journal's Post Ref. column (last step). Account balance = difference between the two sides.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.1.7 Posting the Opening Entry · p.71-74
17853: Historical cost principle: assets are recorded at the price paid. Objectivity: records supported by documents. Business entity, matching, consistency, etc.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.3.1 Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) – The Historical Cost Principle · p.93
17854: A cash journal is a special journal for all cash receipts and payments. Proving cash: beginning balance + cash received − cash paid = ending cash balance (agrees with the last cheque stub).
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.4 Journalizing Transactions in a Cash Journal – 3.4.1 · p.111-112
17855: The trial balance proves equality of debits and credits but does not detect errors such as an equal wrong amount on both sides, omitted or duplicated transactions, or posting to a wrong account of the same type. Fiscal (accounting) period = length of time covered by the analysis.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.5.1 The Trial Balance – Fiscal Period · p.125
17856: Income statement: revenue − expenses = net income for a period. Closing entries transfer balances: revenue → Income Summary, expenses → Income Summary, Income Summary (net income) → Capital, Drawing → Capital. Ending capital = beginning capital + net income − drawings.
17857: Purchase journal: merchandise bought on account (total: Dr Purchases, Cr A/P). Sales journal: merchandise sold on account (total: Dr A/R, Cr Sales). 17867: Transport: road, railway, water, air, pipeline (liquids and gases such as petroleum), ropeway, human- and animal-powered. Modern communication systems: visual, acoustic (telephone, telegraph, record player), telecommunication and data-processing.

17871: Law of demand: price up → quantity demanded down. Exceptions: Giffen and Veblen goods (demand rises with price). Substitutes (sugar–honey) vs complements (car–gasoline). Normal goods: demand rises with income; inferior goods: demand falls as income rises.

17873: TC = TFC + TVC. Fixed costs do not change with output and must be paid even at zero output; variable costs change with output. For TC = a + bQ, TFC = a and TVC = bQ.

17874: Consumer equilibrium: MUA/PA = MUB/PB. A price fall → buy more → MU falls (diminishing MU), giving a downward-sloping demand curve. Indifference curves slope downward, are convex to the origin, higher curves = more satisfaction, and never intersect.

Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.2 Subatomic particles – mass number and atomic number · p.44-45

17895: Molecular mass = sum of atomic masses. % element = (mass of element in formula ÷ molar mass) × 100.

17896: Combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and combustion (a substance burns in oxygen; a hydrocarbon gives CO₂ and H₂O).
Textbook: Grade 9 · 3.4 Types of chemical reactions – combustion · p.127-130

17898: d-block elements from Z = 21 (Sc) to 30 (Zn) in period 4, where the inner third shell is being filled.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.2 Modern periodic table – electron configuration and transition elements · p.14
17899: A single bond shares 2 electrons, a double bond 4, a triple bond 6. Ionic compounds (MgO, NaCl) conduct electricity when molten or dissolved; covalent molecular compounds (CCl₄, CH₄) do not.
17900: Solutions are clear, homogeneous, cannot be separated by filtration and have variable composition; their properties (boiling/freezing point, vapour pressure) differ from those of the pure solvent. Dilute = little solute relative to solvent; concentrated = much solute.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.1 Characteristics of solutions · p.63
17901: Molarity M = moles of solute ÷ litres of solution. Concentration compares particles per unit volume, so halving the volume with half the particles leaves the concentration unchanged.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.3 Concentration of solutions · p.75
17902: The solubility of a solid changes with temperature; pressure affects only gases (Henry's law). All nitrates and sodium salts are soluble; chlorides are soluble except AgCl, PbCl₂, Hg₂Cl₂; CaSO₄ is only slightly soluble.

17904: pH = −log[H⁺]; pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic. Milk of magnesia (Mg(OH)₂) is basic. Common titration indicators: methyl orange, litmus, phenolphthalein. For H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH: mol NaOH = 2 × mol H₂SO₄.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 4.3 The pH scale · p.144
17905: Kinetic energy: energy of motion – thermal and electrical energy. Potential energy: energy of position – chemical and gravitational energy.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 5.1 Energy transformation – kinetic and potential energy · p.154
17906: Exothermic: heat released, ΔH < 0, H(reactants) > H(products) (combustion, respiration, neutralisation). Endothermic: heat absorbed, ΔH > 0 (photosynthesis). A thermochemical equation is a balanced equation with physical states and ΔH – not a skeletal equation.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 5.1 Exothermic and endothermic reactions · p.158-160
17907: Heat of solution = enthalpy change when 1 mol of substance dissolves in water; heat of fusion = heat needed to melt 1 mol of a solid (ice +6.01 kJ/mol); heat of combustion, neutralisation, formation and vaporisation are defined per mole.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 5.2.5 Heat of fusion · p.176
17908: Average rate = Δ[concentration] ÷ Δt (mol/L·s). Rates change as reactants are used up; they depend on concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.1 Rate of a chemical reaction · p.2-4
17909: At equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal and concentrations stay constant. For the exothermic Haber process 3H₂ + N₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, low temperature and high pressure favour ammonia.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.3 Reversible reactions and chemical equilibrium · p.16-17
17910: Oxidation: loss of electrons, increase in oxidation number (addition of oxygen/removal of hydrogen). In Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, Zn is oxidised (reducing agent) and HCl (H⁺) is the oxidising agent. Mn in KMnO₄ is +7.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.1 Oxidation and reduction · p.27-29
17911: Uses: purification of copper, extraction of Na/K (Downs cell for molten NaCl), preparation of chlorine and NaOH from brine (H₂ at the cathode, Cl₂ at the anode, NaOH as by-product), electroplating/protection against rusting.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.4 Electrolysis and its applications · p.53-57
17912: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon (burn to CO₂) but differ: diamond is hard, tetrahedral 3-D network, non-conductor; graphite is soft, layered, conducts electricity. CO combines with haemoglobin far more strongly than O₂, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and stopping oxygen transport.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.2 Carbon – allotropic forms (Table 3.1) · p.71-72
17913: Frasch process: superheated water melts underground sulphur and hot compressed air forces it to the surface. Rhombic and monoclinic sulphur dissolve in carbon disulphide. Contact process: S + O₂ → SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅); SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum); oleum + water → H₂SO₄.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.4 Sulphur – manufacture of sulphuric acid (contact process) · p.107-108
17914: K, Na react vigorously with oxygen and water; metals above hydrogen (Zn, Fe, Mg) displace H₂ from dilute acids; Cu, Hg, Ag, Pt, Au do not. Copper is fairly unreactive, a good conductor, used in wires and coins, and forms brass (Cu–Zn) and bronze (Cu–Sn); Eritrea has large copper deposits.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 4.2 Copper – properties and uses · p.124-125
17915: Metallurgy = extraction of metals from their ores and their purification. Gangue is removed by physical or chemical methods. Roasting: heating a sulphide ore in excess air → oxide + SO₂. Calcination: heating a carbonate ore in limited air → oxide + CO₂.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 4.3 Metallurgy – enrichment of ores · p.126-127
17916: Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (T, n constant). Charles: V ∝ T (P, n constant). Ideal gas equation PV = nRT, so molar mass M = dRT/P.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 5.2 The gas laws – Charles's law · p.170-172
17917: Molecules have negligible volume, no attractive forces, elastic collisions and average kinetic energy proportional to the absolute temperature. An ideal gas obeys the gas laws under all conditions; real gases approach ideal behaviour at high temperature and low pressure.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 5.4 Ideal and real gases · p.186-188
17918: Two bonding pairs and no lone pairs → linear (CO₂, BeH₂, C₂H₂); two bonding pairs and two lone pairs → bent (H₂O, 104.5°).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 1.1 Shapes of simple molecules (VSEPR) · p.6-10

17920: All nuclei with Z > 83 are radioactive; bismuth-209 (Z = 83) is the heaviest stable nucleus. α-decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2 (the parent is the decaying nuclide); positron emission converts a proton into a neutron (Z − 1, A unchanged).
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.1.3 Types of radioactive decay – alpha decay · p.110-111
17921: Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into smaller, highly radioactive nuclei, releasing a large amount of energy; fusion powers stars. Uses: medical imaging and treatment, food irradiation, crime detection, water disinfection. Disadvantages: harmful radiation, damage to cells, waste disposal, reactor maintenance.
17922: Main branches: organic, inorganic, physical, analytical, biochemistry, industrial and nuclear chemistry.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 1.1.2 Branches of chemistry · p.2-3
17923: Atomic number = number of protons; protons + neutrons = nucleons, found in the dense nucleus; electrons move in shells (orbits). The neutron is (slightly) the heaviest particle; the proton is positive.
Textbook: Grade 9 · 2.1.3 Atomic number and mass number · p.44
17924: Metals are lustrous (shiny), malleable, ductile, conductors and lose electrons; sodium is soft, very reactive and not brittle. Non-metals are brittle, non-lustrous, gain electrons and form anions.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 4.1.1 Physical properties of metals · p.117-118
17925: Hydrogen bonds form between molecules with H bonded to a small, very electronegative atom (F, O, N): HF, H₂O, H₂O₂, NH₃. NaH is an ionic hydride (H⁻) and forms no hydrogen bonds.
17926: A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute at a given temperature. Liquid solution: sea water; gaseous: air; solid: brass, bronze, steel.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 3.2 Saturated, unsaturated and supersaturated solutions · p.66-68
17927: Mass % = mass solute ÷ (mass solute + mass solvent) × 100. Molarity = mol solute ÷ L solution. Normality N = equivalents ÷ L; in titrations N₁V₁ = N₂V₂.
17928: Chemical energy is potential energy. Heat flows from the hotter object to the colder one until their temperatures are equal.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 5.1 Forms of energy · p.154
17929: At equilibrium, forward rate = backward rate and concentrations stay constant (not necessarily equal). For aA + bB ⇌ cC, Kc = [C]ᶜ/([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ).
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.5 Chemical equilibrium – equilibrium constant · p.22-23
17930: Amorphous carbon: coke, wood charcoal, animal charcoal, carbon black. CO is colourless, odourless, neutral and a good reducing agent. CO₂ uses: photosynthesis, refrigeration (dry ice), beverages, fire extinguishers.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.2 Carbon – amorphous forms of carbon · p.72-73
17931: Organisms cannot use atmospheric N₂ directly; soil bacteria convert it into ammonium and nitrate compounds that plants use. Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ with an iron catalyst.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.3 Ammonia – Haber process · p.90-91
17932: A strong, dense, oily, highly corrosive acid; concentrated H₂SO₄ is a dehydrating and oxidising agent.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.4 Sulphuric acid – properties · p.108-109
17933: K, Na, Ca react with cold water; Mg with hot water; Al, Zn, Fe with steam; Pb, Cu, Ag, Au, Pt do not react with water at all. Aluminium is light, strong, corrosion-resistant and a good conductor: foil, cans, utensils, aircraft, power cables, window frames.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 4.1.2 Chemical properties – reaction with water · p.122
17934: Gases expand indefinitely, are easily compressed, have low density and diffuse rapidly. The average kinetic energy of the molecules depends only on the absolute temperature.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 5.1 Properties of gases · p.162-163
17935: Alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (C₄H₆); cycloalkanes CₙH₂ₙ (n ≥ 3). Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures; geometric (cis–trans) isomerism needs two different groups on each C of the double bond (1-butene has none). Cracking breaks large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.6 Petroleum – refining and cracking · p.71-72
17936: Nuclear reactions involve protons and neutrons, very large energy changes and loss of mass, and are irreversible. α, β and γ decay are radioactive; ionisation of sodium is a chemical change.
Textbook: Grade 12 · Introduction – Table 3.1 Comparison of chemical and nuclear reactions · p.105-106
17937: Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into lighter, more stable nuclei with release of energy; fusion joins light nuclei.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 3.3 Nuclear fission and fusion · p.122-124
17938: n = mass ÷ molar mass; number of particles = n × 6.02×10²³. Percentage composition = mass of element ÷ formula mass × 100. The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio; it equals the molecular formula when the subscripts have no common factor (CH₄).
17939: Döbereiner (1829) grouped similar elements in triads arranged by increasing atomic mass (middle mass ≈ average of the other two). Group IA = alkali metals, IIA = alkaline earth metals, VIIA = halogens, VIIIA/0 = noble gases.
Textbook: Grade 10 · 1.1 Historical development – Döbereiner's triads · p.2-3
17940: Acids: non-metal oxide + water, direct combination of elements (H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl). Bases: very active metal + water (2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂), metal oxide + water, salt + base. Salts contain the metal cation and the acid's anion (H₃PO₄ → K₃PO₄).
Textbook: Grade 10 · 4.2.3 General methods of preparation of bases · p.127
17941: Increasing pressure (decreasing volume) shifts a gaseous equilibrium toward fewer moles of gas; increasing volume shifts it toward more moles. N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: pressure ↑ → right; volume ↑ → left.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.2.2 Le Chatelier's principle · p.22-24
17942: The less active the metal, the more easily its cation gains electrons (Pt²⁺, Au³⁺, Ag⁺ are discharged first; K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺ last). Coating iron with zinc (galvanising) protects it from rusting.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 2.2.5 Applications of electrolysis; Exercise – protecting Fe from corrosion · p.56, 66
17943: Ammonia is colourless, has a choking/pungent smell, is lighter than air, very soluble and forms a weakly alkaline solution. Haber process N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: controlled by temperature, pressure, concentration and an iron catalyst.
17944: CO, CO₂ and carbonates (CaCO₃) are inorganic. Inorganic: many ionic, ions, high melting points, water-soluble. Organic: mostly covalent, molecules, low melting points, insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents. Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.1.1 Introduction – organic compounds are compounds of carbon · p.25
17945: Hydrogenation (+H₂), halogenation (+X₂) and hydrohalogenation (+HX: HCl, HBr, HI) of alkenes.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.2.3 The alkene series – hydrohalogenation · p.56-58
17946: Q has the same form as K but uses any concentrations. Q < K: too few products, net reaction goes right. Q > K: too many products, net reaction goes left. Q = K: at equilibrium.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 1.2.1 Equilibrium constant and reaction quotient · p.19-20
17947: Sulphur occurs free (Marsa Fatuma, Erta Ale) and as pyrite FeS₂, ZnS, CuFeS₂ and CuS in Eritrea (Debarwa, Adi Nefas). Allotropes: rhombic (stable below 96 °C, octahedral crystals) and monoclinic (stable above 96 °C, needle-shaped).
17948: Water gas = CO + H₂ (steam over hot coke); producer gas = CO + N₂. CO is a reducing agent in metal extraction.
Textbook: Grade 11 · 3.2.2 Carbon monoxide – water gas and producer gas · p.77-78
17949: Members of a homologous series share a general formula (alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) and a functional group and differ by CH₂. Alkyl groups CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ (methyl, ethyl) are side branches. Name from the longest chain and number to give the functional group the lowest locant.
Textbook: Grade 12 · 2.2 Hydrocarbons – homologous series · p.36-38
17950: Scan for the key word, read the whole sentence, and match the paraphrase. Options with ‘only’, ‘certainly’ or changed numbers are usually traps. For NOT/EXCEPT questions, cross out every option the text supports.
17951: A title or main idea must cover the whole paragraph or passage – not a single example (too narrow) and not a general subject (too broad). In well-organised texts each paragraph introduces one idea.
17952: Pronouns and reference phrases point back to the nearest noun that makes sense. Test by replacing the pronoun with each option.
17953: Inference questions ask what the writer implies. Base the answer on explicit clues (e.g. ‘a worldwide issue’ → a worldwide solution), never on outside opinion.
